lesson.title: Iron Rails Everywhere: The Railroad Boom After 1869
lesson.summary: The success of the transcontinental line touched off decades of explosive railroad building that knit the nation into a single market and created the country's first truly big businesses.
lesson.body:
The completion of the transcontinental railroad in 1869 proved that a rail line could be built across enormous distances and turn a profit through land sales and freight traffic. Investors and railroad promoters took notice, and construction accelerated dramatically in the decades that followed. The United States had roughly 35,000 miles of track at the end of the Civil War in 1865. By 1900, that figure had grown to nearly 200,000 miles, making the American rail network the largest in the world. Several more transcontinental routes were completed in these years, including lines controlled by the Northern Pacific, the Southern Pacific, and the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe.

This growth required more than just laying track. Railroads had to solve problems no American business had faced before, because they operated across huge distances and needed to coordinate schedules, safety, and equipment across many independent lines. One major fix was standardizing track gauge, the distance between the two rails, so that cars from one line could run smoothly onto another. Another was time itself: before the 1880s, thousands of local times were kept across the country based on the sun's position, which made railroad scheduling chaotic. In 1883, the major railroad companies adopted a system of four standard time zones across the continental United States, a private industry decision that Congress did not formally adopt into law until 1918 but that Americans followed immediately because the railroads set the schedules everyone lived by.

Railroad expansion also depended on continued government land grants and heavy borrowing, which gave rise to intense financial speculation. Building lines ahead of actual settlement or demand was common, and some companies overextended themselves, contributing to financial panics such as the one in 1873 that followed the collapse of the banking firm Jay Cooke and Company, itself overextended on railroad bonds. Despite these setbacks, the long term trend was consolidation, as ambitious financiers and promoters bought up struggling smaller lines and merged them into larger systems.

The railroads became the first modern big businesses in America. They required more capital, more workers, and more complex management than any earlier enterprise, and they pioneered practices like standardized accounting, professional middle management, and nationwide organization that other industries would soon copy. Because railroads carried the raw materials and finished goods for nearly every other industry, they also created the truly national market that made large scale manufacturing and distribution possible for the first time.

This new power came with new controversies. Railroad companies often charged different customers different rates for similar service, favored large shippers over small farmers, and used their political influence to win favorable treatment from state and local governments. Farmers and small merchants who felt squeezed by these practices began organizing politically in the 1870s, planting the seeds of the regulatory battles that would define the rise of big business in the following decades.
